title: Comprehensions and generators
summary: A comprehension builds a list, dict or set in a single expression.

sections.definition: A comprehension builds a list, dict or set in a single expression. A generator produces values one at a time on demand with yield: it doesn't keep everything in memory (lazy evaluation).
sections.analogy: The comprehension is preparing all the orders and putting them on the counter at once. The generator is a barista who makes the next coffee only when you ask for it.
sections.problem: Loading millions of rows into a list to iterate over them once wastes memory needlessly. The generator processes them in streaming fashion.
sections.code:example:
precios = [12_000, 8_500, 30_000]
con_iva = [round(p * 1.19) for p in precios if p > 10_000]   # [14280, 35700]
por_id = {p.id: p for p in productos}                        # dict comprehension

def leer_pedidos(ruta: str):
    with open(ruta) as f:
        for linea in f:
            yield linea.strip()     # se pausa aquí y entrega un valor

# expresión generadora: paréntesis en vez de corchetes
total_caracteres = sum(len(l) for l in leer_pedidos("pedidos.csv"))
sections.bad:
lineas = [l for l in open("ventas_2026.csv")]   # 4 GB en RAM
total = sum(len(l) for l in lineas)

All the data lives in memory at the same time.
sections.good:
with open("ventas_2026.csv") as f:
    total = sum(len(l) for l in f)   # una línea a la vez

Constant memory, same result.
sections.bridge:typescript: The comprehension is equivalent to chained .filter().map(). Generators exist the same way in JS (function* and yield). Compared to a stream that pushes values to you (push), like an EventEmitter or a ReadableStream, a generator delivers them when you ask for them (pull).
sections.interview: A list comprehension creates the whole list in memory; a generator expression or a function with yield produces the values lazily, one per iteration, and keeps its state between calls. I use generators to process large files or paginated results without loading them completely. You have to remember that a generator can only be iterated once.
sections.myths:
• A generator gets exhausted: the second time you iterate over it, it's empty.
  • (x for x in datos) is a generator, not a tuple.
  • Three-level nested comprehensions: if it can't be read aloud, use a normal for.
  • Calling the generator function runs nothing until the first next().

items.code:
g = (x * 2 for x in range(3))
print(list(g))
print(list(g))
items.why: The generator is exhausted after the first full read.

items.code: print({n: n ** 2 for n in range(3)})
